articles.title: Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections and protests – all you need to know
articles.summary: Protests over refugee seats turn deadly, forcing staggered elections under internet blackout and calls for a boycott.
articles.body:
Pakistan-administered Kashmir is facing its worst political crisis in years after weeks of protests demanding electoral reforms turned deadly.

The protests forced staggered regional elections, with the second of the three-phase vote held on Sunday amid calls for a boycott by local activists and a shutdown of businesses in Muzaffarabad, the region’s main city, and other places.

list 1 of 4 Pakistan-administered Kashmir opens polls in violence-wracked election

list 2 of 4 Protest group says 30 dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir vote unrest

list 3 of 4 Pakistan’s Kashmir votes: Why the election hinges on 12 disputed seats

list 4 of 4 Is Pakistan ‘using India’s playbook’ in Kashmir?

The third and final round of voting is scheduled for August 10.

The protests are led by the Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a banned group pushing for changes to electoral laws and more economic concessions for the region.

The epicentre of the protests is Rawalakot, the headquarters of the Poonch division in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), one of the two regions that comprise Pakistan-administered Kashmir, the other being Gilgit-Baltistan.

The AJK region has its own legislature, but it is not a full-fledged province within Pakistan because of the dispute over the Kashmir territory with neighbouring India.

Muzaffarabad, AJK’s capital, is about 30km (18.5 miles) from the Line of Control, the de facto border dividing Kashmir between Pakistan and India.

Residents and local estimates say the death toll has surpassed 50, including seven law enforcement personnel. No official figures have been released. Protest leaders claim more than 60 civilians have died in less than two months.

There has been a partial internet blackout since June 5, according to NetBlocks, an independent observer.

According to iVerify , the fact-checking wing at the Center of Excellence in Journalism (CEJ) in Karachi, telecommunications are limited and internet connectivity is sparse in AJK.

Protesters are demanding more political rights and an end to policies they believe undermine local representation in the legislature. The government says the movement is threatening public order in the region.

Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director-general of Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of Pakistan’s army, on Friday told a news conference that “Kashmiris hold a special place in Pakistan’s heart” and accused vested interests in India of attempting to create unrest. New Delhi has rejected the allegation.

Chaudhry said the state has the sole authority to use force and that violence by any group was unacceptable. He said the government was exercising “wisdom and restraint” in maintaining peace and stability.

During his press conference, Chaudhry did not mention the number of civilian casualties in the region.

Though the protests started in June, their foundation was laid the month before. Here is a timeline:

Late May 2026: Talks between JAAC and the government in Muzaffarabad collapse over demands to abolish 12 seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly.

The seats in the legislature are reserved for Kashmiri refugees who migrated to Pakistan after 1947 and now live outside the region.

The JAAC says the arrangement allows Pakistan-based political parties to influence the government of Pakistan-administered Kashmir while diverting development funds intended for the region.

June 5: Authorities designate JAAC a “proscribed organisation” under the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014.

Internet and mobile services are suspended across the region, and officials advise nonresidents not to travel to AJK between June 5 and June 20, urging tourists already there to leave.

June 7: The AJK Supreme Court rules that the 12 refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

June 8: Clashes erupt between protesters and security forces in Rawalakot and nearby areas. Regional authorities and local media report that 11 people are killed and several injured, including protesters and security personnel.

Federal paramilitary forces are deployed across the region.

June 9: JAAC calls a regionwide general strike. Markets, schools and public transport shut down across much of AJK.

Mid-June: Weeks of strikes, sit-ins and clashes continue in Poonch division, as the death toll crosses 20. JAAC protests in Rawalakot and nearby areas, while the rest of the AJK remains tense but calm.

July 21: The AJK Election Commission announces a revised three-phase election schedule in response to the unrest. Voting is announced for July 27 in Mirpur division, August 2 in Muzaffarabad division and for the 12 disputed refugee seats, and on August 10 in Poonch division.

July 27: The first phase of voting is held in Mirpur division, with early results favouring Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N). On the same day, thousands join a JAAC-led march from Rawalakot towards Muzaffarabad. Deadly clashes erupt again with security forces.

August 2: The second round of voting is held in Muzaffarabad division amid calls for a boycott and limited access to internet.

Are the protests aimed at JAK’s independence?

No, the protests are being held against the reservation of 12 seats in Pakistan-administered Kashmir’s legislature for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir who now live in other parts of Pakistan.

The JAAC accuses Islamabad of using these seats to manipulate local politics – accusations rejected by the national government.

The JAAC says all seats in the legislature must go to those who actually reside in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, and not to people living in other constituencies scattered across Pakistan.

Experts say the crisis is part of a deeper, long-running debate about governance, political representation, resource allocation and regional autonomy in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

The Jammu and Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC), commonly known as JAAC, is a grassroots coalition of civil society groups, traders, lawyers and activists formed in 2023 in the AJK area of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

Rather than being led by a single figure, the JAAC operates as a coalition with several spokespeople, including Shaukat Nawaz Mir, Sardar Umar Nazir, Khawaja Mehran Arshad and Sardar Aman Khan. Mir was arrested in late June after the regional government banned the JAAC.

Following the ban, authorities placed all four spokespeople on a wanted list, offering a reward of 10 million Pakistani rupees ($36,000) for information leading to their arrests.

The JAAC first staged a protest in May 2023 against soaring electricity bills, alleged smuggling of flour and shortages of subsidised wheat.

The movement reached its first major flashpoint in May 2024 , when protesters marched towards Muzaffarabad. Violent clashes with security forces killed at least five people, including a police officer.

The demonstrations ended after the government agreed to a series of economic concessions, marking a big victory for the JAAC.

In September and October 2025, the JAAC unveiled a 38-point charter of demands and launched a regionwide shutdown, prompting authorities to impose a communications blackout.

The charter remains at the centre of the current unrest. Its demands include economic subsidies, investigations into alleged corruption, improved social services and infrastructure, and the abolition of the 12 reserved assembly seats.

AJK’s incumbent Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore is from the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), which is part of the federal coalition government led by PML-N’s Sharif.

PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, the son of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, says 35 of the 38 demands of the JAAC have been implemented, arguing that the remaining proposals are either unfeasible or blocked by court rulings.

Rights group Amnesty International said on July 28 that at least 40 people have been killed, including 34 protesters and six police and paramilitary personnel. The group has demanded a “transparent investigation” into the use of force against protesters.

Residents and local estimates say the death toll has surpassed 50, although officials have not confirmed the figure.

Amid a partial internet blackout, disinformation has further clouded the situation. Viral videos and images claiming to show staged protester injuries, fake police shootings, and AI-generated evidence have circulated widely.

Fact-checkers at iVerify Pakistan have confirmed some visuals as authentic while debunking others as AI-generated or recycled footage. However, many claims remain difficult to verify due to restricted access and the ongoing communications blackout.

Road blockades have also cut off towns, disrupting travel, work and access to healthcare.

Markets, schools and public transport have repeatedly remained shut during the regionwide strikes, while tourism has suffered after authorities urged visitors to leave.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox: "I think the scariest person in the world is the person withâ¦" - a lesson on humour, perspective and facing hard times with lightness
articles.summary: US News: Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh, and a ser.
articles.body: Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh, and a serious problem often becomes easier to approach once it can be seen from another angle. It can create a little distance from fear, frustration and uncertainty, even when the circumstances themselves have not changed. Michael J. Fox, the actor and Parkinson's disease advocate, put a striking twist on that idea. "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor," he said. Not being able to laugh, in his framing, is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life, and coming from someone who has lived with a serious, lifelong illness for decades, the line carries a good deal more weight than a passing joke.Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox"I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor"Where this quote actually comes fromThis line comes from an interview Fox gave to journalist Amy Wallace, published on Reader's Digest's website. Fox is not really suggesting that a humourless person is dangerous in any literal sense. He is pointing at the seriousness that tends to surround someone who cannot laugh at themselves, cannot recognise irony, and cannot find any lightness in a genuinely difficult moment. Humour creates real distance from a problem. It lets someone acknowledge that something is hard without letting it completely take over.Why humour matters most during genuinely difficult stretchesLife inevitably brings disappointment, uncertainty and real stress. Humour cannot solve every problem on its own, but it can genuinely change how someone responds to one. Being able to laugh during a hard period offers a small emotional break, and it can help people communicate when a direct, serious conversation feels too uncomfortable to actually have. None of this means every situation deserves to be treated as a joke. Humour and genuine seriousness can exist side by side.How humour actually helps people manage stressStress tends to narrow someone's attention down entirely onto the immediate problem in front of them. A moment of real laughter can interrupt that cycle. Research into humour and stress has suggested that positive humour can genuinely influence mood and help people cope with stressful experiences, and laughter itself is linked to physiological changes, including a release of muscle tension. None of this should be overstated. Humour is never a substitute for professional help or a practical solution when someone faces a genuinely serious problem. As an everyday coping tool, though, it can offer a genuinely useful shift in perspective.Why laughing at your own mistakes actually mattersOne of the most valuable forms of humour is simply being able to laugh at your own missteps. Nobody gets everything right. People mispronounce words, misjudge situations and occasionally embarrass themselves, and someone who can acknowledge a mistake without being consumed by embarrassment tends to find it easier to actually learn from it. Self-directed humour also tends to make social interactions considerably more comfortable, since it signals that a person does not expect flawless perfection from either themselves or anyone else around them.Why humour can genuinely strengthen relationshipsShared laughter helps people form real connections. Friends, colleagues and family members often use humour to build a sense of familiarity and trust, and a well-placed joke can break tension that a serious conversation might struggle to shift on its own. There is an important line here worth being clear about, between humour that actually brings people together and humour that humiliates someone else. Jokes built on cruelty or prejudice tend to damage relationships rather than genuinely strengthen them, and the most constructive kind of humour has never really needed anyone else to get hurt.Michael J. Fox's own perspective on adversityFox became one of the most recognisable actors of his generation through films and television, including Back to the Future and Family Ties. In 1991, at the age of 29, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. He later made the diagnosis public and became a prominent advocate for Parkinson's research through the Michael J. Fox Foundation. His public approach to living with the condition has consistently included honesty, genuine optimism and humour, which gives his comments about laughter an extra dimension. His point was never that difficult experiences are inherently funny. It is that holding onto a sense of humour can help someone preserve real perspective while actually facing a genuine challenge. His decades-long relationship with humour, cultivated alongside a chronic illness he never chose, reveals that laughter was never a denial of hardship for Fox, but a deliberate, hard-won tool for maintaining perspective and genuine hope through real adversity.Why humour is not the same thing as avoiding a real problemThere is a meaningful difference between using humour to cope with something difficult and using it to avoid actually dealing with it at all. Some problems genuinely require serious attention and real action, and nobody can simply laugh away financial difficulty, illness or grief. What humour can offer instead is a small amount of emotional breathing space while someone continues addressing the actual underlying issue, which is really the whole distinction worth holding onto here.Why being naturally serious is not actually a flawFox's quote is deliberately provocative, and it should not be read as suggesting that serious people are inherently unpleasant. Some people naturally have quieter personalities, or simply express humour in a different way. The broader lesson is really about flexibility rather than personality type. Someone who can be genuinely serious when it matters, while still finding moments of humour elsewhere, tends to have more ways of responding to life's challenges than someone who treats every single situation with exactly the same level of weight.Other memorable quotes by Michael J. Fox"One's dignity may be assaulted, vandalized and cruelly mocked, but it can never be taken away unless it is surrendered.""I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection.""Family is not an important thing. It's everything.""Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."Why people still find meaning in this quoteHumour is easy to underrate, since it can look insignificant next to more obviously serious qualities like intelligence or discipline. Even so, the ability to laugh genuinely shapes how people communicate, handle their own mistakes and respond to real difficulty. Fox's quote offers a deliberately provocative reminder that life does not always need to be approached with complete seriousness. There will be moments when humour is genuinely inappropriate, and problems that cannot be laughed away at all. In between those moments, though, holding onto a sense of humour tends to keep people connected, flexible and hopeful, which is really the whole point behind the line.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Some people naturally have quieter personalities, or simply express humour in a different way. The broader lesson is really about flexibility rather than personality type. Someone who can be genuinely serious when it matters, while still finding moments of humour elsewhere, tends to have more ways of responding to life's challenges than someone who treats every single situation with exactly the same level of weight.Other memorable quotes by Michael J. Fox"One's dignity may be assaulted, vandalized and cruelly mocked, but it can never be taken away unless it is surrendered.""I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection.""Family is not an important thing. It's everything.""Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."Why people still find meaning in this quoteHumour is easy to underrate, since it can look insignificant next to more obviously serious qualities like intelligence or discipline. Even so, the ability to laugh genuinely shapes how people communicate, handle their own mistakes and respond to real difficulty. Fox's quote offers a deliberately provocative reminder that life does not always need to be approached with complete seriousness. There will be moments when humour is genuinely inappropriate, and problems that cannot be laughed away at all. In between those moments, though, holding onto a sense of humour tends to keep people connected, flexible and hopeful, which is really the whole point behind the line.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The execution of Leslie James, the last woman hanged in Wales
articles.summary: Leslie James was executed for murder, but her looks were talked about as much as her crime.
articles.body:
As Leslie James was marched to the gallows on the morning of her 40th birthday, she could never have known her death would put her name in the history books.

On 14 August 1907 at 08:00, James was led from the women's block of Cardiff Prison to a shed which housed the gallows, suspended above a 15ft-deep (4.5m) pit.

There waiting for her were Henry and Tom Pierrepoint - a surname synonymous with the noose - and with that pull of the lever, James would become the last woman to be hanged in Wales.

In June of that year, she was accused of deliberately smothering a day-old baby girl as part of what the police and press called a "baby farming" conspiracy.

But a new book by author Mary Jones casts doubt on details surrounding the case, highlighting James's previously unreported brain injury, and how her looks were as much the focus of the press attention as her crime.

In The Execution of Leslie James, Jones documents how in the months leading up to her crime, Leslie James, or Rhoda Willis as was probably her real name, was hit by a bike, giving her such severe concussion that she was in hospital for three months.

She argues: "Whatever Leslie's culpability in her crimes, this surely ought to have been taken into account."

James stood trial at the July 1907 Swansea Assizes accused of murdering baby Treasure, who was only identified by the surname of her mother, Maud Treasure from Fleur-de-lis in Caerphilly.

The prosecution claimed James responded to a newspaper advert asking for someone to take care of an unwanted baby, offering £6 initially, and a further £2 at a later date.

At the time, "baby farming", where "inconvenient" children were offered up for money, was seen as a social scandal.

After collecting the child, it was alleged that James smothered her on the train journey back to Cardiff, most likely around Llanishen.

Most damningly for James, evidence emerged that she had previously taken on two other babies in similar circumstances.

After a trial lasting one-and-a-half days, the all-male jury took just 12 minutes to convict her, in what must have seemed like an open-and-shut case in those days.

In passing sentence, the judge said: "Don't let anyone suppose that because you are convicted of murder that nobody pities you, nobody prays for you.

"I implore you to employ the short time that is left to you to prepare for death and for that mercy which you will undoubtedly find in heaven, but which you cannot expect here."

Jones believes there were serious flaws in the trial, most importantly that James's brain injury was not mentioned as an explanation for her reckless behaviour.

"Her barrister, Ivor Bowen, was only appointed on the morning of the trial on the judge's orders and, as such, there was no time to speak to Leslie or call any defence witnesses.

"Had they have done so, then the jury would have heard what baby Treasure's family told the police, that the child was already frothing from the mouth, possibly because of the indigestible sugar-water mix which they had given her because her mother was unable or unwilling to breastfeed her, and also that she had been extremely tightly swaddled, so that neighbours could not tell that the package being handed over to Leslie was a baby.

"Either of these could have led to baby Treasure choking or suffocating, though Leslie didn't help her own defence insofar as she was an alcoholic and, I believe, honestly couldn't recall how the infant died on that journey home."

Jones added that, while James's two previous forays into baby farming were used in evidence against her, the counter argument was never put forward.

She left a note requesting medical assistance for the first child, who she left on the steps of the Salvation Army, and the second was thriving after being adopted by her landlady, Mrs Wilson at 132 Portmanmoor Road in Splott, Cardiff.

On the evening of 3 June 1907 James returned home but couldn't sleep in her own bed, and instead bunked up with fellow lodger Rose Smith.

The following day she went out and got "paralytically drunk".

As Mrs Wilson tried to help her into bed, she discovered a tightly-wrapped parcel, which at first she thought to be a cut of meat, only to discover the truth and informed the police.

"She is most likely to have been born in Sunderland in 1863, though she claimed to have been educated in a London boarding school," said Jones, who believes there may be evidence to support this.

"Rhoda/Leslie appears from the records to have been a highly literate and articulate lady and far removed from the common-or-garden 'hussy' or 'fallen woman' which the press chose to stereotype such so-called baby farmers."

Jones said when James was arrested she gave her name as Leslie James, but on previous public documents she was variously listed as Rhoda Willis/Dalzell/Lascelles, daughter to a jeweller, Ernest Dalzell, which may have provided her with a more affluent background.

While living a "blameless life" prior to the bike accident, by 1907 she had fallen into "troubled ways".

She was locked in a love triangle with Scottish-born brothers Stewart and McGregor McPherson, between whom she bore two babies.

Jones said that by the time she sought lodgings at Portmanmoor Road, she was already deeply damaged.

"The way she sought shelter in Rose Smith's neighbouring room shows that she knew something terrible had happened, but it also lends evidence to the conclusion that she hadn't intended for it to happen.

"Surely, if Rhoda had have been guilty of murder, then she wouldn't have drawn such attention to herself."

Cardiff council, her own solicitor Harry Lloyd, and the general public raised a petition of about 50,000 names to spare her life.

A 1,000-strong crowd outside the prison were mortified when a guard pinned the notice of her death to the gates.

Home Secretary Herbert Gladstone had, the night before, concluded that she be made an example of because of the "despicable practice of baby farming prevalent in south Wales".

Jones said: "I am seeking an apology for the fact that such a troubled woman was hanged without evidence that she'd ever committed murder.

"It is beyond doubt that baby Treasure died while in the care of Rhoda, but her degree of culpability is very debatable, at the very most she is guilty of manslaughter."

Jones said a degree of misogynistic fetishism saw James go to the gallows.

"All the press reports and even the hangman Henry Pierrepoint remarked on her beauty and composure.

"No male's demeanour had ever been commented upon so much in the papers: 'From the way in which the sunlight caught her auburn hair to her composure at the moment the lever was pulled.'

"She was made to stand out for some sort of message."

Now, 119 years after she died, the only physical record of James's grave is an etched cross next to a potato patch within the walls of Cardiff Prison.

articles.title: Hayden Panettiere’s ex-partner Wladimir Klitschko shares ‘profound shock’ in tribute
articles.summary: “She left this world far too soon,” wrote Klitschko, the Ukrainian boxer and father of their child, Kaya.
articles.body: Actor Hayden Panettiere’s former partner said Tuesday their family is “going through a time of profound shock and grief” following her death. Wladimir Klitschko, the Ukrainian boxer and brother of the mayor of Kyiv, paid tribute to his ex-fiancée on Instagram. “The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon,” he wrote. “Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.” Klitschko shared an image of their daughter happily sitting on her mother’s shoulders as he paid tribute to Panettiere’s “incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry.” “Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives. To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was,” Klitschko wrote. “I extend my deepest condolences to Hayden’s parents, her friends, and her fans, who are also grieving today. Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon,” he added. “Rest easy, Hayden. May you find eternal peace.” Panettiere died Sunday at age 36. The Greenville County, South Carolina, Coroner’s Office said Monday that the cause of death is pending further investigation. An autopsy was completed Monday, the statement added, and “no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to the death.” Authorities got a 911 call Sunday around 1:50 p.m. about a “reported cardiac arrest” at an apartment complex, according to the coroner’s office. Police said an acquaintance of Panettiere’s, whom they did not identify, made the call. “The preliminary investigation has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances,” police said in a news release. Panettiere was best known for her roles in the television shows “Heroes” and “Nashville” and had recently published a memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” which generated headlines over its revelations — including some about her past relationships. Panettiere revealed this year that she previously struggled with postpartum depression and addiction, which she said led to her decision to give up custody of daughter Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, her only child, in 2018. Panettiere said she had always wanted to be a mother but discussed her sadness amid her postpartum depression in a tearful interview on the “Jay Shetty Podcast” in May. Despite being apart from her daughter after she gave up custody to Klitschko, Panettiere told Shetty, she formed a strong bond with her. “I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she said. “I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment.” Klitschko and Panettiere announced their engagement in 2013. It was after Panettiere gave birth to their daughter in 2014 that her life began spiraling out of control, she wrote in her memoir. She later went into rehab and reluctantly signed over custody of Kaya to her father when the girl was nearly 3 years old. By 2018, she and Klitschko were no longer engaged. “I still hadn’t processed everything that had happened with Wlad and Kaya, not to mention my anxiety and depression,” she wrote. She detailed the decision to sign over custody, saying that she thought things might change once she got better but that they never did. Panettiere said in interviews that she had developed a good co-parenting relationship with Klitschko, that she was able to visit her daughter in Ukraine and that she regularly talked to her on FaceTime. articles.title: 81,000 warning letters sent to crypto holders in HMRC tax crackdown
articles.summary: According to a Freedom of Information (FOI) request the number of letters sent has almost tripled since 2024.
articles.body:
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) sent more than 81,000 letters warning cryptocurrency holders they may owe capital gains tax in the past year.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) request seen by the BBC showed the number of letters sent by the tax authority had almost tripled since 2024.

Investors could face fines or prosecution if they fail to declare profits they made from selling, even if they exchange one cryptocurrency for another.

New powers due to be given to HMRC next year will make it easier to target wealthy crypto investors, with one analyst saying investigations will be like "shooting fish in a barrel".

"There is the expectation amongst tax authorities that cryptocurrency investment is rife with tax evasion," says Neela Chauhan, partner at UHY Hacker Young - which carried out the FOI.

"A lot of the traders are young, have had little previous exposure to HMRC and often work under the assumption that HMRC has limited visibility over their activities."

In the 2025-26 financial year, HMRC sent 81,172 warning letters, emails and text messages to crypto investors it suspects may have underpaid tax.

An HMRC spokesperson said: "Weâre committed to helping people pay the right amount of tax, and the vast majority do.

"We regularly send letters to educate, remind or prompt customers to review their tax affairs, including customers who use crypto assets."

From Bitcoin to blockchain: Key cryptocurrency terms and what they mean Published 5 June

From Bitcoin to blockchain: Key cryptocurrency terms and what they mean

The value of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum has fallen in the past year, but HMRC suspects there are still large amounts of unpaid capital gains from the rise in cryptocurrency values between December 2022 and October 2025.

During this time, the price of Bitcoin shot up from around Â£14,000 to Â£90,000.

Accountants are urging investors to check whether they owe money, as upcoming powers will make it easier for HMRC to target individuals.

From March 2027, cryptocurrency platforms located in dozens of countries outside the UK will be obliged to share information about their customers with tax authorities.

HMRC said the new powers would force "crypto bros to pay their fair share of tax" when the rules were announced last year.

The tax office estimated the changes would help raise up to Â£315m by April 2030, adding that this was the same amount needed to fund more than 10,000 newly qualified nurses for a year.

"Once HMRC has this data, tax investigations into cryptocurrency investors will be like shooting fish in a barrel," warned Ms Chauhan.

In the last year, the price of Bitcoin has fallen to around Â£48,000.

articles.title: College Fantasy Football: Proceed with caution on these overvalued names for 2026 — Here's Eric Froton's All-Fade Team
articles.summary: Eric Froton goes over players he's avoiding in College Fantasy Football for the 2026 season.
articles.body:
When reading this "Busts" column, it is important to point out that I perceive these players to be overvalued at their current draft position, not that they are outright "off-my-board" unless otherwise specified.

Play Yahoo's new College Fantasy Football game: Create or join a league now!

As I've mentioned in previous columns, pro-style quarterbacks have major difficulty reaching the all-important 20-fantasy-point-per-game mark in Yahoo Standard scoring without a defined rushing component. Running backs in committees are always dicey propositions, and it's vital to target receivers and tight ends who are targeted downfield in pass-friendly offenses.

With that, here are the most overvalued players currently being selected in Yahoo Standard Leagues.

Please understand this "Bust" label pertains to Yahoo Standard scoring where pro-style signal-callers are depreciated by way of 4-point passing touchdowns. Philosophically, we've seen Ohio State morph from the up-tempo attack of Ryan Day's formative head coaching years, to the glacial offense we witnessed last year that slowed OSU down to the 135th slowest pace in the country.

The Buckeyes now bring in the infamous run-heavy NFL castoff Arthur Smith to run the offense. With Sayin having run the ball just 31 times for 27 yards and zero rushing touchdowns last year, and new OC Smith nerf-ing the entire offense, I don't think Sayin gets enough work in the run game to clear the 20-FPPG benchmark that is imperative in 1QB leagues. Pass on Sayin, and vulture a pair of high-upside QBs who are capable of cracking the 400 rushing yards barrier in the later rounds.

This is not to disparage the exceptional job Dickey did for the Red Raiders last season after USC transfer Quinten Joyner sustained an injury that knocked him out for the year. However, this year Joyner is healthy and expected to be an established rotation member who will eat away at Dickey's 200-touch workload from a year ago. Compounding matters is the continued presence of passing down maven J'Koby Williams, who cranked out 1,254 total yards over 14 games last year, and dual-threat QB Will Hammond who will siphon gold zone touches. Dickey is an abnormally risky investment for a player who produced 1,037 yards and 13 touchdowns in the 2025 regular season thanks to the increased competition for touches.

The truly most disappointing CFF news of the offseason has been the unfortunate gunshot wound in his leg that Hardy suffered back in May. While there was initial optimism that Hardy would return in short order, he did not dress for the team's most recent scrimmage. With Missouri starting the season with four very favorable matchups against Arkansas-Pine Bluff, Kansas, Troy and Mississippi State, it's entirely possible we don't see Hardy in any meaningful capacity until at least October, and even that is speculative. I've drastically dropped him in my rankings and am outright avoiding Hardy unless we get some form of tangible positive camp news heading into Week 1.

We've seen Marsh being selected in the top-25 of Power Conference receivers this offseason, in the hopes that the new Utah-imported coaching staff will ply him with a swarm of targets, despite rave reviews about Utah transfer WR, JJ Buchanan. However, QB Bryce Underwood struggled in spring and is expected to have a more Devon Dampier-like effect from a fantasy perspective, utilizing his legs as much, or more, as his arm. With Michigan playing one of the top-five toughest schedules nationally and deploying a run-first ethos in the defense-oriented Big Ten, Marsh is a risky proposition inside the top-25 of P4 drafts.

Staley is a solid, but relatively uninspiring, wideout who was used as departed UT QB Jesse Aguilar's safety valve underneath last year. Just 9.6% of Staley's targets traveled 20+ yards downfield for a very conservative 8.1 average target depth. With Tennessee's field stretcher on the outside, Chris Brazzell, now in the NFL, I expect Mike Matthews to expand upon his 25.3% deep target rate and inherit Brazzell's vacated downfield targets after receiving just 74 looks last year compared to Brazzell's 99. I recommend passing on Staley and taking Matthews 2-3 rounds later according to current draft trends.

It was a storybook season for the Blue Devils in 2025, as Duke somehow managed to finagle their way into a thrilling overtime ACC championship game victory against Virginia last year. The bad news is superstar QB Darian Mensah and WR Cooper Barkate are at Miami, while former starting WR Que'Sean Brown is at Virginia Tech. The only key offensive cogs who return are their workhorse running back and Hasley, and all the news coming from camp points to a return to their run-first ways behind Sheppard now that the best QB they've had since Daniel Jones is gone. The scheme shift and QB downgrade craters Hasley's CFF appeal, as he spent 60% of his reps inline last year and Duke will experience a significant downgrade from their 35 PPG scoring average last year. Leave him on the waiver wire and take high-upside shots elsewhere later in drafts.

Rutgers fielded the dirt-worst fantasy defense in the country last year, as the Scarlet Knights got throttled by superior Big Ten competition. While Raymond was a certifiable workhorse who logged a massive 244-carry workload in 2025, he was sparsely used in the receiving game. While he caught seven passes for 88 yards in a fluke explosion against Washington, he only registered 11 catches for 137 yards in his other 11 contests.

Also muddying Raymond's profile is the fact he scored nine touchdowns in his first five games, feasting on the likes of Miami (Ohio), Ohio and FCS Norfolk State before punching in just four scores over his last seven games. It's not hard to find starting running backs in the early season when P4 teams are feasting on their G6/FCS underlings, but Raymond presents startability issues against the better defenses on Rutgers' B10 schedule such as USC, Indiana, Michigan, at Wisconsin and at Penn State.

Raymond has been selected in the top-six of several of P4 drafts I've witnessed and participated in, and is a first rounder in the vast majority of leagues. I think Raymond should be viewed as a late-second rounder due to his startability issues, lack of a consistent receiving workload, and his sizable production splits when facing quality Big Ten programs.

Running backs in committees are always dicey propositions, and it's vital to target receivers and tight ends who are targeted downfield in pass-friendly offenses.
With that, here are the most overvalued players currently being selected in Yahoo Standard Leagues.

Please understand this "Bust" label pertains to Yahoo Standard scoring where pro-style signal-callers are depreciated by way of 4-point passing touchdowns. Philosophically, we've seen Ohio State morph from the up-tempo attack of Ryan Day's formative head coaching years, to the glacial offense we witnessed last year that slowed OSU down to the 135th slowest pace in the country.

The Buckeyes now bring in the infamous run-heavy NFL castoff Arthur Smith to run the offense. With Sayin having run the ball just 31 times for 27 yards and zero rushing touchdowns last year, and new OC Smith nerf-ing the entire offense, I don't think Sayin gets enough work in the run game to clear the 20-FPPG benchmark that is imperative in 1QB leagues. Pass on Sayin, and vulture a pair of high-upside QBs who are capable of cracking the 400 rushing yards barrier in the later rounds.

This is not to disparage the exceptional job Dickey did for the Red Raiders last season after USC transfer Quinten Joyner sustained an injury that knocked him out for the year. However, this year Joyner is healthy and expected to be an established rotation member who will eat away at Dickey's 200-touch workload from a year ago. Compounding matters is the continued presence of passing down maven J'Koby Williams, who cranked out 1,254 total yards over 14 games last year, and dual-threat QB Will Hammond who will siphon gold zone touches. Dickey is an abnormally risky investment for a player who produced 1,037 yards and 13 touchdowns in the 2025 regular season thanks to the increased competition for touches.

articles.title: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could âweaponiseâ the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that âbetter senseâ would prevail to pr.
articles.body: Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could âweaponiseâ the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that âbetter senseâ would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained âuntouchableâ for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance âunilaterally."â...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,â Iqbal told the Asia Society.âWe (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,â the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth âbulgeâ, describing the region as the âleast integratedâ in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a âdirect responseâ for putting the IWT in abeyance.âIndia proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,â Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their âred lineâ and threatened India over the move, describing it as an âact of war.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Positive approach': Bangladesh ministers on possibility of joining Mecca pact
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladesh maintains a positive approach towards joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, two junior mini.
articles.body: Bangladesh maintains a positive approach towards joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, two junior ministers have said, while stressing that any decision would be guided by the countryâs national interests.Signed in Saudi Arabiaâs Mecca on August 7, the pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all three.Humayun Kobir, Bangladesh's newly appointed state minister for foreign affairs, told state-run BSS that the Bangladesh Nationalist Party government is pursuing a âBangladesh Firstâ policy and a âbalanced foreign policy with national interests at its coreâ, which could lead Dhaka to join the defence pact.âBangladesh maintains a positive approach towards the possibility of joining an economic or defence framework involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, taking into account its own interests and the changing dynamics of the global economy and trade,â Kobir said.He further stated that Dhaka would also strengthen bilateral ties with Islamabad through normal diplomatic engagement, with a focus on trade and people-to-people connectivity. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected to visit Riyadh at the invitation of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and the tour schedule is likely to be finalised after the summer, he added.Another state minister for foreign affairs, Shama Obaed Islam, in a separate media interaction, supplemented Kobirâs comments, saying Bangladesh's national interest and the interests of its people would determine Dhakaâs stance on joining the agreement.âWhether we join any pact or any multilateral body will be decided primarily on whether Bangladesh's interests and the interests of the Bangladeshi people are protected.âThe two junior ministersâ comments came two days after PM Rahmanâs finance and planning adviser, Professor Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, described the government's âBangladesh Firstâ policy as a âparadigm shiftâ in the countryâs foreign policy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cafes, shops shut over 'violation of norms': Iran's hijab crackdown returns as women defy veiling rules
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran's long-running debate over mandatory hijab has resurfaced as hardliners push for stricter enforcement, even as the country grapples with the fall.
articles.body: Iran's long-running debate over mandatory hijab has resurfaced as hardliners push for stricter enforcement, even as the country grapples with the fallout of its conflict with the US.During the height of the conflict, women without headscarves were seen at pro-government gatherings and in state media, suggesting that authorities were reluctant to enforce the rules amid more pressing concerns.In recent weeks, however, conservative clerics and politicians have intensified calls for a crackdown on âpublic nudityâ. State media have reported the closure of cafes, restaurants and shops accused of failing to enforce mandatory dress rules.Businesses face action over hijab rulesOn July 19, at least seven cafes and restaurants in Tehran were shut down for allegedly failing to enforce the mandatory hijab, according to human rights group HRANA. The group has also documented social media accounts being blocked over alleged violations of public dress codes, according to CNN.Authorities have used terms including âviolation of normsâ, âviolation of modestyâ and âfailure to observe Islamic decencyâ in such cases. In one case, HRANA said a boutique was closed âdue to unveilingâ.The Tehran Prosecutor's Office has also warned of serious action against alleged âindecencyâ at cafes, restaurants and shops selling clothing considered inappropriate.In South Khorasan province, 10 cafes were closed over alleged violations of âsocial norms and mandatory hijab rulesâ, the Mehr news agency reported, citing the province's chief prosecutor.State media have meanwhile carried repeated calls from religious leaders for women to observe the hijab, describing it as part of Iran's cultural identity.Women continue to defy rulesThe renewed push comes nearly four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in police custody sparked the nationwide âWoman Life Freedomâ protest movement. Amini had been detained over allegations that she was improperly dressed. The protests were violently suppressed, but widespread defiance of compulsory hijab rules has continued, particularly among young women.There have been several high-profile cases. In June, Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and eight members of her band and production team were sentenced in Qom to 74 lashes and banned from leaving the country for two years. Ahmadi had appeared with uncovered hair and bare shoulders during a livestreamed performance in 2024.Women have also increasingly appeared without headscarves in public and on social media. Videos showing groups of women riding motorcycles without hijabs have circulated online, including footage from Tehran, Shiraz and Isfahan.One Instagram post by a group of women in Shiraz said, âWeâre the motorcycle girls of Shiraz! Shiraz girls, letâs go!â Another post showed around 20 female motorcyclists in Isfahan and described it as âthe biggest female motorcycle event in Isfahan.âPezeshkian questions crackdownIranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has questioned whether stricter laws can change people's behaviour, suggesting that authorities should focus on cultural engagement instead.Referring to an interview with a conservative cleric, Pezeshkian said, âThe cleric mentioned hijabâ¦ Well, there are neighborhoods, there are mosques, go and work on it there! Can you really change peopleâs behavior through laws?âHe also referred to disagreements with his daughter over the issue, asking, âDoes it mean I should force her?!â âChanging behavior is a cultural matter; itâs about belief. You canât create belief in people through force,â he added.Former MP Gholamali Jafarzadeh Imanabadi has similarly argued that officials should focus on inflation and people's livelihoods rather than the hijab.Hardliners demand tougher actionHardliners, however, have stepped up pressure on the government to enforce the rules. Kayhan editor Hossein Shariatmadari has described enforcement as both a legal obligation and a religious duty.According to CNN, a member of Iran's parliament, Mohammad-Taqi Naqdali, said, âWe see what the state of nudity and public vice is like in our midstâ¦Israel and America cannot destroy us, but this decay that has plagued our religious culture and is spreading nudity in a disastrous and widespread manner in society will.âIran's Islamic Penal Code criminalises appearing in public without âIslamic hijabâ, although it does not precisely define the term. A tougher law approved in 2024 proposed expanded penalties and surveillance, but its implementation was halted following intervention by the Supreme National Security Council.For now, authorities appear cautious about launching a full-scale street crackdown. A Tehran woman in her 60s told CNN that women were openly wearing clothes such as crop tops and shorts and that headscarves had become rare.âI donât think they can make these girls wear headscarves again. But then again, thatâs also what we thought when the revolution happened. We never thought they would be able to force us to wear them, but in the end, they did,â she added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Shein aims for almost $27bn valuation in stock market debut
articles.summary: The fast-fashion giant's shares are due to start trading in Hong Kong on 1 September.
articles.body:
Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September.

The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of the firm, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China.

Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries.

The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends.

Shein said in a filing on Monday that it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 ($6.07; £4.45) and HK$49.50 each.

At the top of the range, the share sale would raise $1.77bn (£1.3bn) for the company and give it a market valuation of $26.8bn.

But that is much lower than the $100bn it was worth in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs.

The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan.

The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023.

Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University.

Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said.

Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added.

Shein's listing will test investor confidence in the fast-fashion industry and its position in an increasingly competitive market.

In July, Shein said it had swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty waiver on small packages called the de minimis exemption.

The company said it lost $99m in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier.

It also came as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused.

"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said at the time.

How can you reduce your fashion footprint?

The truth behind your $12 dress: Inside the Chinese factories fuelling Shein's success

The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets.

The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing.

Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will affect Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market.

Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption .

The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes.

These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added.

Jane Foley, Rabobank's head of FX strategy, told the BBC's Today programme that the ending of the de minimis exemption "really did undermine the core business model of Shein", adding that the EU has done something similar.

Richard Lim of research firm Retail Economics said Chinese retail giants such as Shein have caused "a huge wave of destruction" in markets like the UK, with more established companies struggling to compete.

The British retail industry believes Shein is "not playing on a level playing field", he told the BBC.

It is expected that the UK will impose similar restrictions as the US and EU on small packages from Chinese retailers in 2028.

As of the end of March 2026, Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders.

But its fast-fashion business has faced concerns over its environmental impact, and allegations of forced labour in supply chains. The company has previously told the BBC it has a "zero tolerance for forced labour".

Its attempt to go public on the London Stock Exchange collapsed after the company came under scrutiny over its refusal to answer questions about its supply chain practices .
paragraphs: Fast-fashion giant Shein could see its stock market valuation reach almost $27bn (£19.8bn) when its makes its debut in Hong Kong on 1 September.

The long-awaited move comes after failed attempts to list in the US and London due to regulatory challenges amid scrutiny of the firm, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China.
Since it was founded in 2008, Shein has risen to become one of the world's biggest fast-fashion retailers, with customers in more than 150 countries.
The e-commerce giant is known for selling ultra-cheap clothes, backed by a vast network of factories in China that are able to quickly manufacture new products based on the latest trends.
Shein said in a filing on Monday that it will offer nearly 280 million shares for between HK$47.60 ($6.07; £4.45) and HK$49.50 each.
At the top of the range, the share sale would raise $1.77bn (£1.3bn) for the company and give it a market valuation of $26.8bn.
But that is much lower than the $100bn it was worth in 2022, reflecting weaker sales growth and higher costs.
The initial public offering (IPO) is being backed by Wall Street investment giants Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JP Morgan.
The company will make its highly anticipated debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after efforts to go public since 2023.
Hong Kong has been revived as "one of the largest IPO markets" after attracting more firms from mainland China, said economics associate professor Feng Qu from the Nanyang Technological University.
Shein is likely to command a higher valuation in Hong Kong than it would in London, where regulatory scrutiny derailed its plans to sell shares there, Feng said.
Chinese companies may also be wary of selling shares in the US as tensions between the world's two largest economies could result in firms being de-listed, he added.
Shein's listing will test investor confidence in the fast-fashion industry and its position in an increasingly competitive market.
In July, Shein said it had swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty waiver on small packages called the de minimis exemption.
The company said it lost $99m in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier.
It also came as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused.

"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said at the time.
How can you reduce your fashion footprint?
The truth behind your $12 dress: Inside the Chinese factories fuelling Shein's success
The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets.

The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing.
Some investors are questioning whether higher costs and regulatory challenges will affect Shein's ability to get goods swiftly and cheaply to market.
Marguerite LeRolland from market research company Euromonitor International told the BBC that the firm's sales have slowed in the US partly due to the end of the de minimis exemption .
The exemption helped retailers like Shein and its fierce rival Temu grow quickly in the US as they were able to deliver goods without incurring import taxes.
These factors could "narrow the price gap" between Shein and competitors like Primark and H&M, she added.

Jane Foley, Rabobank's head of FX strategy, told the BBC's Today programme that the ending of the de minimis exemption "really did undermine the core business model of Shein", adding that the EU has done something similar.

Richard Lim of research firm Retail Economics said Chinese retail giants such as Shein have caused "a huge wave of destruction" in markets like the UK, with more established companies struggling to compete.
The British retail industry believes Shein is "not playing on a level playing field", he told the BBC.
It is expected that the UK will impose similar restrictions as the US and EU on small packages from Chinese retailers in 2028.
As of the end of March 2026, Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders.

But its fast-fashion business has faced concerns over its environmental impact, and allegations of forced labour in supply chains. The company has previously told the BBC it has a "zero tolerance for forced labour".

articles.title: In 1953, a Hong Kong imam brought eight date palms from Mecca; one survived and later officials changed a road route rather than cut it down
articles.summary: China News: In 1953, an imam named Ai Pok-tak returned to Hong Kong from a pilgrimage to Mecca carrying eight date-palm saplings, hoping to grow a piece of his fa.
articles.body: In 1953, an imam named Ai Pok-tak returned to Hong Kong from a pilgrimage to Mecca carrying eight date-palm saplings, hoping to grow a piece of his faith in a city where the tree was rarely seen. Only one survived. Planted outside the family's home near Hong Kong's border with mainland China, it eventually grew to more than twice the height of the family's two-storey house. Ai and his wife, Ma Yuk-lan, had moved to Hong Kong from Gansu province in 1949, and the palm's survival became deeply intertwined with their family's faith and history. Decades later, the same tree became the centre of a long-running dispute over road construction. What began as an effort to save the palm from demolition under British colonial rule continued after Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, with Ma repeatedly asking authorities to find a way to preserve it.How British colonial officials agreed to reroute a road around the palmAccording to the Los Angeles Times, Ma first faced the threat of losing the tree in 1972, when British colonial authorities planned a road that would have required its removal. She recalled appealing to David Akers-Jones, who was then serving in the New Territories administration, and asking that the road be shifted slightly instead of cutting down the palm. Ma and her family pleaded with officials to spare the tree, and the road was ultimately rerouted, allowing the date palm to remain where it had grown for decades. The distinction over Akers-Jones' position is important: he did not become Hong Kong's Chief Secretary until 1985, so that later title should not be attributed to him when describing the 1972 episode.Why the date palm became so important to the familyThe tree's importance extended beyond its unusual presence in Hong Kong. Date palms have a strong cultural and religious association with Islam, and dates themselves hold an important place in Muslim traditions. Retired senior imam Cheung Kwong-yee told the Los Angeles Times that Islamic clerics do not regard date palms as formally sacred, but acknowledged their considerable symbolic significance within the faith. The palm also became a living connection to Ai's journey from Gansu to Hong Kong and to the family's pilgrimage history. After the original group of eight saplings was reduced to one surviving tree, its continued growth gave the family a tangible link to the place from which Ai had brought it.Why Hong Kong authorities wanted the palm removed againThe tree faced another threat after Hong Kong returned to Chinese sovereignty in 1997. Authorities eventually told Ma that it would have to be removed to make way for road widening. Government engineer Fun Yat-fu said he knew of only two date palms in Hong Kong at the time, highlighting the rarity of the species in the territory. Ma resisted the proposal and explored alternatives, including asking whether the palm could be moved to land behind her home rather than being destroyed. She also approached her landlord about relocating it elsewhere on his property, but securing permission from the wider family associated with the land proved difficult. Officials offered another option: transplanting the palm to a public park. For Ma, however, moving the tree away from the place where it had grown for decades was not an equivalent solution.The family kept looking for a way to save the treeAs the deadline for dealing with the palm approached, Ma continued pressing authorities to reconsider. She even wrote to Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa asking whether the tree could be preserved behind her home. The family's attachment to the palm had also grown through the natural changes around it. Ma described two smaller trees that had appeared near its base without being deliberately planted. She believed they had helped stabilise the larger palm against Hong Kong's powerful typhoon winds. The dispute also produced an unusual coincidence. Akers-Jones, the official whom Ma remembered helping save the palm decades earlier, was himself facing a road project that threatened his seaside home and a large banyan tree on his property.For Ma, the date palm was more than an obstacle in the path of a road. It was a surviving link to her family's past, a symbol of faith and a tree that had already outlasted one government decision to remove it. The family's decades-long effort to protect it showed how a single tree can become intertwined with questions of heritage, religion, memory and the rapidly changing landscape of Hong Kong.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: âYou are powerful, but remember 1971?â Pakistani politician takes fresh swipe at Army
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistani politician and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army, recalling the militar.
articles.body: Pakistani politician and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army, recalling the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh, then known as East Pakistan.ââWe are the protectors of this country. No oneâs father can harm this country.â I agree, you are very powerful,â Rehman remarked at a JUI (F) convention in Peshawar, targeting Pakistanâs top military leadership.He recalled how the Pakistan Army laid down its arms in 1971, just a day after then-President and military ruler General Yahya Khan declared that it would fight until the end."But I remember, and maybe there are some elders who remember, that in December 1971, one day before laying down arms, General Yahya Khan addressed the army and said, we will fight in the streets, in the deserts, in the fields, in the factories, in the mountains, and we will fight against them. We will fight. We heard these big words then," Rehman added.The JUI-F further chief questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive" to their misery.âWhy are you putting the country and the people to the test? Why are you having fun when your public is suffering? And today is 2026. When the revolution came in Afghanistan in 1989, and the war started, now you tell me, itâs been 45-46 years, blood has been flowing on the same line for about half a century. When blood flows like this, then it is a sign of geographical changes,â Rehman remarked.Warning that persistent state oppression and ongoing conflict threaten the nationâs integrity and could signal territorial disintegration, he stated, âIt is a sign of oppression. Then at least inform us of your intentions. We are tolerating it and will continue to tolerate it. It will continue. A few more days, my dear, just a few more days. We are forced to take a breath in the shade of oppression. If we endure the oppression for a little longer, if we suffer, if we cry, it is the legacy of our ancestors. We are helpless.âRehmanâs remarks came days after he challenged the military to enter politics directly, declaring, âIf you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish.â(With ANI inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir spoke to Donald Trump ahead of Tehran visit: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spoke with US President Donald Trump last week, days before his planned visit to Tehran, according to thr.
articles.body: Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spoke with US President Donald Trump last week, days before his planned visit to Tehran, according to three Pakistani sources cited by Reuters.The previously unreported call came as Washington prepared to impose major economic sanctions targeting Iran and countries that trade with Tehran. It remains unclear what Munir and Trump discussed.Munir is scheduled to travel to Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian leaders as Islamabad steps up efforts to revive stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran.Iran's foreign ministry announced Munir's visit on Sunday, saying he would discuss bilateral relations and regional issues with Iranian officials.He will be accompanied by a delegation expected to hold high-level meetings with the Iranian leadership.The visit comes as Pakistan seeks to revive diplomatic efforts between the United States and Iran after an interim agreement aimed at creating a 60-day window for high-level peace talks broke down last month.Pakistan had signed the agreement as a guarantor and has since been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to the negotiating table.Pakistan has increased its diplomatic engagement with Iran in recent weeks. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran earlier this month and met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that Munir's visit would focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation and supporting efforts to promote peace and security in the region.The Pakistani government has not officially commented on Munir's reported conversation with Trump.The reported Trump-Munir call comes as Washington steps up pressure on Tehran.Trump warned on August 20 that the United States would launch what he called the âmost crushing economic operationâ against Iran if Tehran failed to reach a deal.Pezeshkian on Sunday defended the June agreement, describing it as the best way for Iran to move beyond a situation of âneither war nor peaceâ.At the same time, Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's new hard-line head of the Supreme National Security Council, warned neighbouring countries against joining any renewed US campaign targeting Iran's economy.The earlier negotiations collapsed after tensions between Washington and Tehran escalated in mid-July, following renewed military strikes.Pakistan's mediation efforts have so far failed to produce a breakthrough, with the Strait of Hormuz remaining a major obstacle amid disruptions to one of the world's most important energy shipping routes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
articles.summary: His comments come as the government urged TikTok and other social media firms to remove wrong-way driving videos.
articles.body:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv, Burnham said the people who share footage glorifying dangerous driving are "doing something that's truly reprehensible".

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it prohibits posts encouraging participation in high-risk challenges, including driving against traffic, and takes down such content once made aware.

It said it also restrict users under 18 from seeing content not suitable to them, such as posts depicting any sort of reckless driving.

The BBC has also contacted X for comment.

On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.

At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."

Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".

He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.

"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."

The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.

A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".

They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."
