Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."
He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".
"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.
Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a head-on collision in County Kildare, Ireland, after driving the wrong way down a motorway.

They hit a car which was believed to be carrying a family heading to the airport for a holiday. As of Friday, three women and a seven-year-old boy were still in hospital where they were being treated for serious injuries.
At the time, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly called it "irresponsible and dangerous driving".

He said: "What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."
Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live, Pollard said he wanted to see social media companies "step up".
He added: "It's one of the reasons they've argued against some of the regulations, saying they can police themselves.
"Well this is the perfect opportunity to demonstrate it. Remove the content that celebrates dangerous behaviour on our roads."
The minister said the government will use powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take down any content that remains online.
A spokesperson for regulator Ofcom said under the act platforms "must minimise children's exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges".
They added that in July, it launched an investigation "into TikTok's compliance with its child safety duties, and we've shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

articles.title: Bundelkhand: Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
articles.summary: Rising heat and water scarcity are deepening old caste inequalities in Bundelkhand region, activists say.
articles.body:
A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.

Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.

The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.

Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.

Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.

She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.

"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.

Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.

Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.

The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.

A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.

Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.

As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.

"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.

"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."

Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.

Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.

Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.

"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.

Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.

"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.

Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.

There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.

Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.

About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.

He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.

"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.

In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.

"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."

Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.

"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.

"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."

Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.

Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.

The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.

Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.

"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.

The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.

"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.

The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.

There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.

Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.

Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.

More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.

That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.

In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.

When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

articles.title: France tornado: Village of Pomas ravaged and dozens hurt
articles.summary: The south-western village of Pomas was hardest hit, with hundreds of homes damaged and fifteen people taken to hospital.
articles.body:
A tornado has torn through the village of Pomas in south-west France, injuring 39 people and damaging hundreds of homes.

Authorities said 15 people were taken to hospital and two were in a critical condition. One man said his pregnant wife was injured after their house collapsed on her.

More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the village south of Carcassonne after winds reaching 117km/h (73mph) tore roofs off houses and damaged an estimated 300 homes on Monday.

"Half the village has been destroyed," said one resident called Pierre, who described the tornado as swirling like a "huge red and yellow chimney".

"There's a huge castle and a third of it is has collapsed - even though these are stones that have stood for 1,000 years," Pierre told Ici Occitanie.

The third stage of the Vuelta a España cycle race, which was taking place in the Aude area of south-western France, had to be cancelled when a hail storm forced the riders to take shelter about 15km from the finish line.

The extreme weather has left about 2,800 homes across 10 villages without electricity, according to officials.

Local sub-prefect Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand told French radio that she was not aware of anyone missing. She lowered the number of victims from 41 to 39, and said 15 of them had been treated in hospital.

"I heard this massive noise... then I saw everything flying around in the air and my roof collapsed over my head," shocked resident Chantal told French radio. "I've got no house left, that's for sure... I was really scared. I thought that's it, this my final hour."

French authorities had issued an orange alert for thunderstorms in large parts of the country's south-west, which have already been hit by power outages and transport disruptions.

Eyewitness footage from the region captured the swirling vortex of the tornado looming in the horizon above houses and trees.

Images from the small village of Pomas, which was the hardest hit, showed uprooted trees, damaged cars and rubble from destroyed homes.

Meanwhile there were flight delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and north of Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.

On average, France experiences several dozen tornadoes per year, according to the country's national weather service Météo-France.

It comes after Europe's summer of unprecedented heatwaves and wildfires, with France's south-west region among the worst affected with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.

articles.title: Medieval Guernsey reading habits revealed in hidden manuscripts
articles.summary: Archivists discover 17 manuscript fragments from medieval times were repurposed as book covers.
articles.body:
Seventeen fragments of medieval manuscripts that had been "hidden in plain sight" for centuries have been uncovered in Guernsey.

Offering insight into the island's early literary culture, the fragments suggest late medieval Guernsey was home to keen readers, and reading in French rather than English was preferred.

Also regarded as "striking early examples of recycling", historians found the fragments were repurposed as covers for notebooks and bindings for administrative records, meaning they were unknowingly preserved.

Prof Tamara Atkin, a book historian from the University of Oxford, said the discovery "transforms what we can now say about Guernsey's medieval manuscript culture".

Until now there had been virtually no evidence for libraries, collections of books or literary culture in the island during the medieval period, said the States of Guernsey.

Atkin said the discovery showed "books of several kinds - scholastic, liturgical, and literary - were available on the island" at the time.

The fragments - found in the Island Archives and His Majesty's Greffier's strongroom - were identified by the archive team working alongside Atkin and manuscript expert Dr David Rundle, from the University of Kent.

It began when archival assistant Callum Tostevin-Hall was asked to track down a 16th Century copy of Edward III's 1331 Extente of Guernsey, which detailed the Crown's rights in the island.

During his research, he noticed the shelfmark contained a reference to a vellum cover with Latin text that had been removed from the notebook in a previous round of conservation.

"I checked this cover and was astonished to find that it was clearly a reused bifolium from a medieval manuscript," he said.

"Taken together the fragments give an unprecedented glimpse into Guernsey's medieval past, which is not only very exciting for the Island Archives as an institution, but also for me personally as a medievalist."

The team said many of the fragments were in Latin but six of them were in French, with most being popular works that survive in several copies across England and France.

One comes from a dramatic poem called L'Estoire de Griseldis, a secular play thought to have been written by Philippe de Mézières around 1395.

Versions of the Griselda story were popular across late medieval Europe but the version found in the Guernsey fragment was said by the team to be "exceptionally rare".

Island archivist Vikki Hart said the reuse of the fragments as book covers showed resourcefulness "is nothing new in Guernsey".

"What was once a practical act of reusing old parchment has, centuries later, preserved pieces of the island's history that would otherwise have been lost," she said.

articles.title: Man City to launch formal bid for Enzo Fernández as deadline nears, testing Chelsea’s £120m resolve
articles.summary: Manchester City are set to send a formal bid to Chelsea for Enzo Fernández before next week's transfer deadline.Fernandez is Manchester City's leading transf...
articles.body:
Manchester City are set to send a formal bid to Chelsea for Enzo Fernández before next week's transfer deadline.

Fernandez is Manchester City's leading transfer target before the closure of the window, with the club preparing to test Chelsea 's resolve with a bid.

Chelsea had agreed with Fernandez that the midfielder could leave if his £120m asking price was met but set a deadline of August 14th for a deal.

City failed to meet that figure before the deadline, but believe a deal can be done in the final days of the window.

Enzo Fernández keen on Etihad move: Man City prepare imminent offer after missing Chelsea's deadline

Fabrizio Romano is reporting that City will submit an offer for the Argentina international imminently. Fernandez is keen on the move to the Etihad, where he would reunite with former Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca.

Maresca wants to add Fernandez to a midfield group that has been depleted by the departures of Bernardo Silva , Rodri , and Tijjani Reijnders , while Nico Gonzalez is nearing a move to Newcastle United .

Fernandez was named among the substitutes for Chelsea's 3-2 win at Fulham on Monday and appeared as a second-half substitute at Craven Cottage.

Chelsea are insistent that the club will only consider his sale now if they receive a huge offer and can improve their squad.

A £120m fee would represent a club-record deal for Manchester City, eclipsing the £116m fee paid to sign Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest earlier this summer. The Cityzens are also finalising the £85.4m arrival of Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille .

articles.title: In 1972, Lyndon and Lady Bird Johnson gave the Texas White House and about 600 acres to the US but kept lifetime rights; she continued living there until 2007
articles.summary: US News: In 1972, former US President Lyndon B Johnson and his wife, Lady Bird Johnson, gave their ranch house and about 600 acres of land to the National Park.
articles.body: In 1972, former US President Lyndon B Johnson and his wife, Lady Bird Johnson, gave their ranch house and about 600 acres of land to the National Park Service for use as a national historic site. However, the couple retained a 'life estate', which allowed them to continue living at the property during their lifetimes.According to Seattle Times, the ranch, near Stonewall, Texas, became known as the 'Texas White House' during Johnsonâs presidency. He used the property as a retreat from Washington and hosted foreign leaders and other important visitors there. It also became a place where he held meetings and spent time away from the White House.The main house did not immediately became open to the public. The Johnsons retained the right to use the home, and after Lyndon Johnson died in January 1973, Lady Bird Johnson continued to live there under the arrangement. She remained connected to the ranch for the rest of her life.Lady Bird Johnson died in July 2007 at the age of 94. Her death ended the lifetime arrangement and allowed the National Park Service to take over the main house. By then, much of the ranch was already open to visitors.Story of the âTexas White HouseâLyndon Johnson bought the property from his aunt in 1951. During his presidency, it became closely linked to his time in office. The ranch offered Johnson a place away from Washington where he could work and meet visitors.He served barbecue to world dignitaries there and hosted several foreign heads of state. Staff meetings were also held outside, under the shade of a large oak tree.The property, however, was more than a place connected to Johnsonâs presidency. Lady Bird Johnson called it her 'heartâs home'. âIt was always Lyndonâs favorite time, particularly around sunset, from the earliest spring until cold weather drove us in,â she once said.Lady Bird Johnson also appeared to think about what would happen to the home after her family was gone. In 1965, after visiting Thomas Jeffersonâs Monticello, she spoke about looking at the Johnson house differently.âI did find myself looking at the house with new eyes, the eyes of someone who someday might leave a simple house, not anything so great in our history as Monticello, but one to which other generations of American tourists might come,â she said.Seven years later, the Johnsons made the property part of the public historical record. In December 1972, they gave the ranch house and hundreds of acres to the public as a national historic site, while retaining their life estate.Lady Bird Johnson's time at the ranchThe donation became especially significant after Lyndon Johnson died on January 22, 1973, at his LBJ Ranch. Under the terms of the life estate, Lady Bird Johnson could continue to live on and use the property, including the ranch house, for the rest of her life.She had a house in Austin, but the ranch remained important to her. A longtime family friend, Neal Spelce, said she returned to the property as often as she could. âShe would get away to the ranch as often as she could. It really was her home,â Spelce said.The ranch was already being visited by members of the public, but the main house remained off-limits while Lady Bird Johnson lived there. Visitors could take tours through the property and walk up to the family cemetery. Lady Bird was also known to sometimes wave at tour buses passing by.Spelce said the ranch had a relaxed atmosphere despite its connection to the presidency. âThere really was no pretense. It was a place where you felt you could take off your shoes and kick your feet up,â he said.Lady Bird Johnson continued to live at the ranch part-time until her death in 2007. She was buried beside Lyndon Johnson in the familyâs private cemetery, less than a mile from the ranch house.Home prepared for public toursAfter Lady Bird Johnsonâs death, the National Park Service was set to take over the 4,000-square-foot ranch house. The Johnson family was given time to remove personal belongings before officials began preparing the home for public tours.Officials considered recreating much of the interior so that it would look as it did between 1963 and 1973, when Lyndon Johnson was president. They also wanted the presentation to reflect Lady Bird Johnsonâs life at the ranch after her husbandâs death.The house itself had grown considerably over the years. Its original section was a one-room cabin with a loft built by German immigrant William âPolecatâ Meier. By 2007, it had become a 28-room building with eight bedrooms and nine bathrooms.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Cavers heard wind roaring from beneath a rubble-choked pit in New Mexico; after years of digging they broke through in 1986, and more than 145 miles of Lechuguilla Cave have since been mapped
articles.summary: US News: For decades, Lechuguilla Cave was just a footnote in New Mexicoâs Guadalupe Mountains: a 90-foot entrance pit leading to 400 feet of dry, dead-end pas.
articles.body: For decades, Lechuguilla Cave was just a footnote in New Mexicoâs Guadalupe Mountains: a 90-foot entrance pit leading to 400 feet of dry, dead-end passages that had once been mined for bat guano. But in the 1950s, cavers began noticing something strange: wind roaring up from the rubble-choked floor, hinting at hidden passages below. Acting on that hunch, a team of Colorado cavers obtained permission from the National Park Service and began digging in 1984. On May 26, 1986, they broke through into vast walking passages, launching one of the most significant cave discoveries in modern history. This article draws on the National Park Serviceâs official history of Lechuguilla Cave.From a forgotten pit to a world-class caveBefore 1986, Lechuguilla was considered a small, fairly insignificant historic site in the backcountry of what is now Carlsbad Caverns National Park. A mining claim filed in 1914 supported a year of guano extraction from the entrance passages, after which the cave was visited only infrequently. The persistent sound of wind moving through the rubble convinced different cavers over the years that there had to be more cave below, even though no obvious route existed.When the Colorado team started digging in 1984, they were chasing that sound, and the possibility of a major system. Their breakthrough in 1986 opened not just a new passage, but a new chapter in American speleology. What followed has been described as some of the worldâs most exciting cave exploration, taking place in one of the finest known caves on the planet.145 miles of mapped passages and a record-breaking depthSince that first breakthrough, explorers have mapped more than 145 miles (233 km) of passages in Lechuguilla Cave and pushed its known depth to 1,604 feet (489 m). As of July 2019, Lechuguilla ranks among the ten longest caves in the world and is one of the four longest in the United States. It also holds the distinction of being the second deepest limestone cave in the country.These numbers tell only part of the story. The caveâs sheer scale, combined with its intricate network of rooms, shafts, and corridors, has drawn cavers from around the globe. They come for the challenge of unexplored passage and for the chance to move through a landscape of never-before-seen beauty, carefully surveying and mapping each new section as they go.A gallery of rare formations and otherworldly beautyLechuguilla Cave quickly revealed that its importance went far beyond length and depth. Explorers found large deposits of gypsum and lemon-yellow sulfur, along with a fantastic array of rare speleothems, cave formations created by mineral deposition. Some of these features had never been documented anywhere else in the world.Among the highlights are 20-foot gypsum âchandeliers,â delicate 20-foot gypsum hairs and beards, and soda straws reaching 18 feet in length. The cave also contains hydromagnesite balloons, cave pearls, subaqueous helictites, rusticles, and unusual looped formations known as u-loops and j-loops. In terms of size, depth, and variety of speleothems, Lechuguilla surpassed its nearby sister, Carlsbad Cavern, though no single room discovered so far in Lechuguilla is larger than Carlsbadâs famous Big Room.A natural laboratory for geology and microbiologyBeyond its visual splendor, Lechuguilla Cave has become a valuable scientific laboratory. For the first time in the Guadalupe Mountains, a cave extends deep enough to allow scientists to study five separate geologic formations from within the same system. The abundance of gypsum and sulfur supports the idea that much of the cave was formed by sulfuric acid dissolution, a process in which acidic waters dissolve limestone to create large voids.Researchers also believe the cave hosts rare, chemolithoautotrophic bacteria, microbes that essentially âeatâ rock by feeding on sulfur, iron, and manganese minerals. These organisms may play a role in enlarging the cave and shaping some of its unusual speleothems. Other studies suggest that some of these microbes could have medicinal qualities beneficial to humans, adding another layer of importance to protecting the caveâs fragile ecosystem.Why access is tightly controlled and why that mattersLechuguilla Cave lies beneath a designated wilderness area within the park, but its passages come very close to adjacent Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land. Oil and gas drilling on BLM-managed areas could potentially leak gas or fluids into the cave, killing cave-adapted life, destroying delicate formations, and threatening the safety of people inside.To minimize these risks, the National Park Service actively manages the cave and surrounding karst resources. Access to Lechuguilla is limited to approved scientific researchers, survey and exploration teams, and NPS management-related trips. This restrictive policy helps preserve both the caveâs extraordinary geology and its unique biological communities, ensuring that the system revealed by that roaring wind in the 1950s remains intact for future study and, in carefully controlled ways, exploration.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and does not own supercars in photos, lawyers claim
articles.summary: Prosecutors argue Tate and his brother Tristan are a flight risk and should not be released on bail.
articles.body:
Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.

Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.

They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny.

Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.

In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention".

"The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.

At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues.

"The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says.

"But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

Prosecutors argued that both brothers "have significant resources available to them, both in terms of money and in social media networks," adding they also have shown a "propensity to intimidate vulnerable complainants".

Prosecutors also cited social media posts made by Andrew Tate, in which he allegedly mocked prosecutors and suggested he could hide his identity to avoid arrest.

The superyacht referenced is not owned by the Tates and they were paid to promote it, the submission says.

Cars, including an Aston Martin and Bugattis which featured in social media content, were rented, it says.

"The Tates are engaged in several businesses 'teaching' men how to earn money. It is in their interest to portray themselves on social media as uberwealthy," it adds.

US Marshals arrested the brothers in Miami last month after the Crown Prosecution Service in the UK brought 38 new charges, including rape and offences related to sex trafficking, against them.

They are now facing a total of 59 charges relating to alleged offences between July 2010 and August 2017.

Andrew, 39, and Tristan, 38, have both previously denied any wrongdoing.

The brothers are dual British-US citizens and spent part of their childhood in Luton.

Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Tate first rose to fame after an appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother in 2016.

A former kickboxer, he has millions of social media followers and has appeared in countless videos flaunting what appears to be an ultra-luxurious lifestyle.

articles.title: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise
articles.summary: The US says new sanctions are an "economic D-Day", but Tehran's leaders have survived restrictions before.
articles.body:
The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.

Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.

His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?

Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.

What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.

The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.

The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.

If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.

They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.

Washington has also left little room for diplomacy.

Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.

It was already in deep trouble before the war, with high inflation and a rapidly weakening currency, and has deteriorated further since the fighting began with US and Israeli air strikes on 28 February.

The weakening of the Iranian currency, the rial, is felt sharply and widely. Imports cost more, businesses struggle to plan, and people's savings lose value. Restrictions on oil exports also reduce the government's access to foreign currency.

Negin - not her real name - is a 34-year-old woman who says her monthly income is now about $100 (£73). She told the BBC: "I don't go to the cinema, theatre, or concerts. I don't buy gifts for anyone. I don't attend birthday parties. I can only buy meat with the government subsidy voucher; otherwise, I wouldn't be able to afford it."

Mona, a housewife with two kids, says her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war. She adds: "We feel scared, especially after the sanctions that began yesterday. Ever since the war, my spouse has not gone back to work. He used to work on ships."

She adds: "We're trying to manage our expenses as best we can, but we've definitely had to cut back on all of our extra spending and small luxuries."

Iran may believe time is working against US President Donald Trump. Further disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could push oil and petrol prices higher, add to US inflation and become a political problem before the US midterm elections in November.

That gives Tehran an obvious date to watch, but relying on American elections is a gamble.

Iran's economy could be much weaker by then.

And beyond the midterms lies another problem. With Trump not seeking re-election in 2028, his outgoing administration may feel it has more freedom to continue the confrontation with Iran and accept the costs.

Iran is, therefore, watching two clocks.

One is political and runs in Washington. The other is economic and runs inside Iran. Every month of lower oil exports, disrupted trade and pressure on the rial makes waiting for a deal to end the war more expensive.

That leaves Iranian leaders with a difficult choice. Making concessions now could look like surrendering under pressure and strengthen hardliners who say Washington will only demand more.

Waiting could improve Iran's position if Trump's strategy runs into political or economic problems. But Tehran could also find itself negotiating later with a weaker economy.

Much now depends on what happens outside Iran.

If Chinese banks, regional trading partners and companies start pulling back because they believe Washington will punish them, Bessent's campaign may change Tehran's calculation.

If they do not, the opposite could happen. Those Iranians arguing against compromise will say Washington has played another supposedly decisive card without changing the balance and that Iran should continue to wait or resist.

How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran?

That gives Tehran an obvious date to watch, but relying on American elections is a gamble.
Iran's economy could be much weaker by then.

And beyond the midterms lies another problem. With Trump not seeking re-election in 2028, his outgoing administration may feel it has more freedom to continue the confrontation with Iran and accept the costs.
Iran is, therefore, watching two clocks.

One is political and runs in Washington. The other is economic and runs inside Iran. Every month of lower oil exports, disrupted trade and pressure on the rial makes waiting for a deal to end the war more expensive.
That leaves Iranian leaders with a difficult choice. Making concessions now could look like surrendering under pressure and strengthen hardliners who say Washington will only demand more.
Waiting could improve Iran's position if Trump's strategy runs into political or economic problems. But Tehran could also find itself negotiating later with a weaker economy.
Much now depends on what happens outside Iran.
If Chinese banks, regional trading partners and companies start pulling back because they believe Washington will punish them, Bessent's campaign may change Tehran's calculation.

If they do not, the opposite could happen. Those Iranians arguing against compromise will say Washington has played another supposedly decisive card without changing the balance and that Iran should continue to wait or resist.
How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran?

articles.title: Swedish military seeks to take over Russian-owned estate near naval base
articles.summary: The armed forces request the seizure of the plot near Muskö Naval Base citing threats from Russian drones.
articles.body:
Sweden's armed forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russia-owned property near a naval base on security grounds.

The military requested the seizure of the beach plot near Muskö base in Stockholm archipelago, citing "the threat from Russian drones and the ownership situation of the property".

Swedish reports say a businessman with links to the Russian state, has been building a luxury house on Muskö island – although his wife, who holds both Russian and Swedish citizenship, is the registered owner.

Two years ago, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined Nato because of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In its statement, the military said the location had "unique conditions for strengthening the defence of Muskö Naval Base, particularly against drones".

The development of Russian drone warfare has "changed the threat landscape for Sweden", the military added.

Public broadcaster SVT said the property has been "a thorn in the armed forces' side".

Defence Minister Pål Jonson said the country needed to "make sure there's no risk of anyone gaining visibility into the site or any kind of tactical edge", Sweden's TV4 reported.

The armed forces' statement quoted Chief of the Defence Staff Carl-Johan Edström as saying that Sweden was "facing the most serious security situation since the end of World War Two".

It is unclear whether the Russian businessman is currently living in Sweden.

His wife is reported to have owned the property since 2017.

articles.title: Man Utd complete £70m deal for Carlos Baleba
articles.summary: Manchester United have announced the arrival of midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton and Hove Albion.Multiple reports claim that the deal has been finalise...
articles.body:
Manchester United have announced the arrival of midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton and Hove Albion .

Multiple reports claim that the deal has been finalised for an initial fee of £65m which has the potential to rise by a further £5m to take the overall value of the transfer to £70m.

Baleba has signed a five-year contract at Old Trafford which includes the option to extend by a further season.

The 22-year-old leaves the Seagulls three years after arriving from Lille and after making 112 appearances on the south coast.

A full international with Cameroon, Baleba missed Brighton 's opening games of the season with an ankle issue.

articles.title: Colombia orders raids targeting migrants without legal status
articles.summary: Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella ordered police and immigration authorities to begin to identify and deport migrants without legal status.
articles.body:
Aug. 25 (UPI) -- Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella ordered police and immigration authorities to begin to identify and deport migrants without legal status, starting in Barranquilla, the president's office said.

De la Espriella issued the order during a security council meeting in the Caribbean city, where he announced measures to combat homicide, extortion, drug trafficking and other crimes, according to an official statement .

"The order to Migration is clear: coordinated operations with the police must begin in Barranquilla to find illegal immigrants," De la Espriella said.

The president said authorities would first target foreign nationals committing crimes and then those who have not regularized their immigration status in Colombia.

"This is a presidential order that must begin to be carried out this week," he said. "I will not accept illegal immigrants, regardless of where they come from, who are committing crimes in Colombia. They will leave, and we will deport them."

De la Espriella said the measure was a political and administrative decision by his government. However, the announcement did not include a decree, an enforcement protocol or a deportation target.

The government also has not explained whether the order changes existing legal standards or seeks to intensify enforcement already carried out by Colombia's immigration authority.

Deportations and expulsions were already part of Colombia's immigration policy. Between August 2022 and June, Migration Colombia documented 3,389 deportations and 2,576 expulsions -- a total of 5,965 people.

The leading reasons for deportation during that period were remaining in the country without legal status, with 1,380 cases, and entering or leaving the country illegally, with 1,315, according to Migration Colombia .

Other cases involved fraudulent documents, false statements, unauthorized activities, court orders and threats to national security or public order. The immigration authority said deportations and expulsions require individual administrative proceedings.

The decision fulfills a campaign promise. In June, when he was still a candidate, De la Espriella said foreign nationals who entered Colombia legally would receive guarantees, while those who violated immigration rules would be returned to their home countries, El Colombiano reported.

Colombia is home to more than 2.8 million Venezuelans, the country's largest foreign population. Migration Colombia had registered 2,831,561 Venezuelan nationals intending to settle in Colombia as of Aug. 31, 2025, according to an official report .

The Association of Venezuelans in Barranquilla called on authorities to respect due process and the right to a defense during the new operations.

"Anyone who commits a crime must answer to the justice system, regardless of whether they are Colombian, Venezuelan or any other nationality," the organization said. However, it warned that "irregular immigration status is not synonymous with criminality," according to Caracol Radio.

articles.title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
articles.summary: The latest escalation in an ongoing trade war between the US and Canada will see new levies on goods from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and makeup.
articles.body:
Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend.

The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; Â£15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday.

The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September.

It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable.

Finance Minister FranÃ§ois-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday.

"Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond."

Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic".

He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat.

Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border.

Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices.

Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US.

But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released.

Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner.

The White House released a statement after Canada announced its counter-tariffs, saying that the US was prepared to offer Canada "the most preferential market access of any country on Earth" in recent trade talks.

"Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection," it said.

In a series of Tuesday posts on Truth Social, Trump also accused Canada of "ripping off" the US for decades and of charging American farmers steep tariffs.

"I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote. "They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!"

He suggested that he will change the name of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes on the US-Canada border, to Lake America, writing: "We don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer."

Trump threatened this week to hike US tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% as of 1 January.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by accusing Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canadian industries including the automobile manufacturing and steel and aluminum sectors.

Public rhetoric on both sides reached a fever pitch on Monday, but some officials struck a more diplomatic tone on Tuesday with hopes that talks could be resumed.

After calling Trump a "loser" on Monday at a news conference, Ontario Premier Doug Ford acknowledged in an interview with CNN that "things got a little heated".

"But I want to make a deal â a good deal for the American people, a good deal for Canadians," Ford said.

The escalation also puts into question the future of a North American free trade pact between Canada, the US and Mexico called the USMCA.

President Claudia Sheinbaum had despatched her economy secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, to Washington for emergency talks after trade negotiations collapsed with Canada.

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump Published 23 hours ago

How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war Published 1 day ago

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

Canada released on Tuesday a list of nearly 900 US products that will be hit by its counter-tariffs.

A 50% tariff on steel and aluminum products that were previously only subject to a 25% counter tariff

A 50% tariff on various other goods including natural honey, furniture, clothing and apparel, makeup and perfume

A 25% tariff on goods including appliances, like dishwashers and washing machines, dairy products, such as cheese, fish and seafood, and certain steel and aluminum derivative products

A 15% tariff on certain types of tools and machinery, including forklifts and air conditioning machines

Canadian officials said they chose products that consumers and businesses in Canada could source elsewhere in an attempt to minimise hurt at home.

articles.title: Kenneth Walker is the latest addition to the Kansas City Chiefs' growing injury list ahead of preseason Week 3
articles.summary: The Kansas City Chiefs' injury list added another starter with preseason Week 3's game with the Seattle Seahawks just a few days away.
articles.body:
The Kansas City Chiefs ' injury list added another starter with preseason Week 3's game with the Seattle Seahawks just a few days away.

The Kansas City Chiefs added a concerning new injury to the report on Tuesday, Aug. 25. Chiefs PR informed reporters during Tuesday media availability that RB Kenneth Walker was added to the injury report with a foot injury. As a result, the team did not expect him to participate in practice on Tuesday. Walker did participate in practice on Monday, following the preseason Week 2 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . That suggests this is a new injury that was suffered during the practice week. The other players expected to miss practice on Tuesday:

We won't hear any specifics about Walker's injury until Andy Reid speaks to the media on Wednesday. The Chiefs have been very cautious with injuries this offseason, notably dialing some guys back when necessary.

Chiefs RB Kenneth Walker's injury history raises concerns here

Injuries have been a major subplot in Kenneth Walker's NFL career so far. It's one of the biggest reasons people doubt his ability to be a workhorse running back in Kansas City. Walker missed Week 1 of his rookie season in 2022 due to a hernia. He suffered an ankle sprain later in the year that kept him out of a divisional game. In 2023, he suffered an oblique injury along with groin and shoulder injuries. He also missed several different stretches of the 2024 NFL season due to ankle, calf, and oblique injuries. The foot injury is something new, and it's rarely a good injury for a running back to deal with. Even if it's minor, it can easily be aggravated. However, the timing is a bit of a saving grace.

The timing is the good news about this injury

The Kansas City Chiefs open the 2026 NFL season on Monday Night Football against the Denver Broncos . Their Week 1 matchup is 22 days away. Walker doesn't need to participate in preseason Week 3. He'll be anxious to participate because it's against his former team, the Seattle Seahawks. The team can simply put him on ice, let the foot injury heal, and hope that he's ready to get back out there for Week 1 of the regular season. That's, of course, if the injury is determined to be nothing serious that would keep him out for a longer stretch of time. Thankfully, the Chiefs do have some talented depth behind Walker this season in Emari Demercado , Emmett Johnson, and Brashard Smith .

articles.title: Trump administration to revoke visas of short-term visitors seeking asylum
articles.summary: The state department says the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to revoke the visas of foreign nationals who entered the US as short-term visitors and later applied for asylum.

"Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud - which is grounds for visa revocation," US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said.

Pigott said the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and would be carried out on a rolling basis. US media reports suggest hundreds of thousands of visas could be affected.

Since President Donald Trump took office, his administration has revoked more than 175,000 visas held by foreign nationals on various grounds, according to the State Department.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio's leadership, we are making clear that a visa is a privilege — not a right," Pigott said in a statement to the BBC.

He said that the department is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then filed for asylum to stay permanently.

"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home," he said.

Those who apply for those so-called short-term B1 and B2 visas are asked to pledge that they will not apply for asylum in the US.

Holders of B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, who have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, will be revoked, the Associated Press reported, citing State Department documents.

The majority of business and tourism visas in 2024 were issued to citizens from Brazil, which obtained more than 1.1m B1 and B2 visas, mainland China, India and Pakistan, according to State Department data.

Just over 32,300 were issued to visitors from Great Britain and Northern Ireland in 2024.

Earlier this month, the state department said it had revoked more than 175,000 visas from foreign nationals who it said "violated the terms of their visas, committed crimes, called for violence against US citizens, defrauded Americans, abused our immigration system, or endangered national security".

articles.title: Dolly Parton, iconic American singer and songwriter who shaped country music, dies at 80
articles.summary: US News: Dolly Parton, the legendary American country singer, songwriter and actress, died on Tuesday aged 80, her family said.Parton was one of the most succe.
articles.body: Dolly Parton, the legendary American country singer, songwriter and actress, died on Tuesday aged 80, her family said.Parton was one of the most successful figures in country music, selling more than 100 million records worldwide and winning 11 Grammy Awards, including a Lifetime Achievement Award. Her most famous songs include "Jolene", "Coat of Many Colors" and "I Will Always Love You".Born on January 19, 1946, in Tennessee, Parton grew up in a poor family and was one of 12 children. She began writing songs when she was about six years old. Her first known song, "Little Tiny Tasseltop", was about a corncob doll made with corn-silk hair."I loved that little doll," Parton wrote decades later. "I expressed myself and my feelings through writing - Iâm sure what I was âthinking was, 'Well, Tasseltop has to have a song about her.'"She received her first guitar at eight and began performing on local radio at 11. At 13, she appeared at the Grand Ole Opry, a famous country music venue and radio programme in Nashville.After finishing school, Parton moved to Nashville to pursue music. She became a regular performer on singer Porter Wagoner's television show and recorded 14 top-10 duets with him. She wrote "I Will Always Love You" when she left the show to start her solo career. The song later became a global hit after Whitney Houston recorded it for the film "The Bodyguard".Parton also became a successful actress. She starred in films including "9 to 5", "Steel Magnolias" and "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas". She received Oscar nominations for songwriting for "9 to 5" and "Travelin' Thru".She wrote an estimated 3,000 songs during her career, with 25 reaching No. 1 on the Billboard Country chart. She was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.Parton also built a business and entertainment empire, including Dollywood theme park in Tennessee.Her philanthropic work included a children's literacy programme that reached families in the US and several other countries. In 2020, she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University for Covid-19 vaccine research, which supported work connected to Moderna's vaccine.Parton was married to Carl Dean from 1966 until his death in 2025. He generally stayed away from the public spotlight."I love to write poetic songs and sing flowery words," Parton wrote in her book "Dolly Parton, Songteller". "I like to make you see something visually, so I want to âpaint a picture. And I love to come up with clever lines, not just like a songwriter, but like a poet."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1903, rabbits were released on Hawaiiâs Laysan Island as a food source; within a decade they had nearly stripped it bare, and three of its five landbird species eventually went extinct
articles.summary: US News: When German immigrant Max Schlemmer brought a small number of domestic rabbits to the isolated Pacific atoll of Laysan in 1903, he hoped to create a p.
articles.body: When German immigrant Max Schlemmer brought a small number of domestic rabbits to the isolated Pacific atoll of Laysan in 1903, he hoped to create a profitable meat-canning business. He also saw the animals as a source of entertainment for his children while he worked on guano extraction operations. Instead, the decision caused one of the worst ecological disasters in modern conservation history. Within a decade, the rabbits had stripped much of the island of its vegetation and eventually helped drive three of its five unique landbird species to extinction. Historical records preserved by the PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine National Monument show how quickly the rabbit population grew across the isolated 1,000-acre atoll. With no natural predators and an enormous appetite, the rabbits consumed vegetation faster than the island could replace it. Over the next 20 years, the uncontrolled population destroyed 26 native plant species, including the unique Laysan fan palm (Pritchardia) and native sandalwood trees (Santalum ellipticum). A once-green habitat for birds was gradually turned into a landscape of bare sand.Devastating losses among native birdsThe destruction of the island's vegetation had a severe effect on its native birds. Before non-native mammals arrived, Laysan supported huge seabird colonies and five species of landbirds that existed nowhere else in the world. As shrubs, tussock grass and trees disappeared, so did insects and places where birds could shelter and nest. The loss of vegetation contributed to the extinction of three endemic birds: the Laysan millerbird (Acrocephalus familiaris familiaris), Laysan rail (Zapornia palmeri) and Laysan honeycreeper (Himatione fraithii). Scientific records from the 1923 Tanager Expedition documented the final days of the Laysan honeycreeper. The expedition was organised by the US Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Biological Survey and the Bernice P. Bishop Museum. Ornithologist Alexander Wetmore recorded that the last three Laysan honeycreepers died during a severe sandstorm while scientists were on the island trying to remove the remaining rabbits. The small, flightless Laysan rail survived for a time on nearby Midway Atoll after birds were introduced there in 1891. However, that population was later wiped out during World War II after rats were accidentally introduced to the atoll. This resulted in the complete extinction of the species.Narrow escape for surviving speciesOnly two of Laysan's endemic landbirds survived the crisis: the Laysan finch (Telespiza cantans) and the critically endangered Laysan duck (Anas laysanensis). Both species survived partly by changing what they ate. They began feeding on carrion, abandoned seabird eggs and brine flies around the island's central hypersaline lagoon. According to a historical overview and restoration plan from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the Laysan duck population fell to dangerously low levels during the habitat destruction. By the early 20th century, fewer than 20 birds were believed to remain in the world. As the damage spread across the Northwestern Hawaiian Archipelago, President Theodore Roosevelt took action. In 1909, he issued an executive order creating the Hawaiian Islands Bird Reservation. Federal authorities later removed Schlemmer from Laysan following indictments linked to illegal feather collection and the unauthorised introduction of invasive species.Eradication and recoveryBy 1918, the rabbits had consumed much of their own food supply. Only a few hundred starving animals remained on an island with badly damaged vegetation. The crisis finally ended in 1923, when the Tanager Expedition arrived on Laysan with armed field crews tasked with finding and killing the remaining rabbits. After the rabbits were completely removed, the US Fish and Wildlife Service began long-term habitat restoration work. Conservation efforts continue today under the PapahÄnaumokuÄkea Marine National Monument. Over the following decades, native bunchgrass (Eragrostis variabilis) and coastal shrubs slowly returned. Their growth helped stabilise the soil and reduce the sandstorms that had threatened the island's central lagoon. Conservationists have also reintroduced related plant species and created protected populations of the surviving Laysan duck and Laysan finch on other protected atolls, including Midway and Eastern Island. To help replace an extinct bird, federal wildlife managers also moved the closely related Nihoa millerbird (Acrocephalus familiaris kingi) from Nihoa Island to Laysan in 2011. The new population became established successfully, marking an important step in rebuilding an island ecosystem that had been severely damaged by a small group of domestic rabbits introduced more than a century earlier.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Expert witnesses challenge claim that Lindsay Clancy experienced psychosis
articles.summary: One more day of testimony expected as closing arguments set for Thursday and jury likely begins deliberations Friday
articles.body:
One more day of rebuttal testimony was expected this week in the trial against Lindsay Clancy, followed by closing statements likely on Thursday.

The jury, which will likely begin deliberations on Friday, will decide whether the Massachusetts mother was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children in January 2023.

On Tuesday, prosecutors put two expert witnesses on the stand who challenged the arguments made by Clancy's defense team – specifically, that Clancy committed the acts while suffering from postpartum psychosis – a mental illness that can cause hallucinations, mood swings, delusions and more, and was hearing a voice compelling her to do it. Her attorney Kevin Reddington has also claimed Clancy had bipolar disorder and was overmedicated.

Tuesday's testimonies capped off more than a month of testimony in a trial that has largely depended on opposing views from experts about Clancy's mental health and her ability to understand the gravity of what she was doing. It's not disputed that she strangled the children – Callan, 8 months, Dawson, three years old, and Cora, five years old, before she allegedly jumped from a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed from the waist down. But the outcome of the trial hinges on questions surrounding Clancy's mental state at the time of the children's deaths. The burden of proof is on the prosecution to show Clancy was not suffering from "a mental disease or defect" and that she had enough capacity to understand "the wrongfulness or criminality of her conduct".

Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors, initially took the stand on Friday and continued his testimony on Tuesday morning. He told the court he "did his best to have an open mind", when he evaluated Clancy in April and that he believed she was "criminally responsible" for the deaths.

Related: Lindsay Clancy trial: psychologist says he doubts claim she was hallucinating

"She retained an awareness of the illegality of killing others, including her children," he said. "Her moral awareness of this killing was influenced by her strong desire to die and, if she was dead, not to leave her children behind."

Over nearly three days of testimony, the prosecution also focused on the timeline of events during the killings, asking Heilbrun to identify whether each step Clancy took was a decision – including her action to take the children down to the basement – in an attempt to convince the jury that these were planned murders. For each, he answered that they did.

Under cross-examination, Heilbrun's told the court he had been paid roughly $54,000 for the 180 hours he has worked on the case on behalf of the state, and that he will likely be paid more as the trial goes on. He also told Reddington that he didn't have experience with postpartum mental health conditions.

A recess was called at one point, after several heated exchanges between Heilbrun and Reddington during which Clancy's attorney accused the psychologist of not reading her medical reports.

Heilbrun's testimony on Monday prompted a request for a mistrial from Reddington after the psychologist mentioned Clancy's Catholic faith. The request was denied, but Judge William Sullivan admonished Heilbrun for the comment and instructed the jury to disregard the reference to "the religion that the defendant was raised with", calling it "an absolutely inappropriate area of testimony".

After Heilbrun left the stand on Tuesday afternoon, prosecutors called forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, who is affiliated with the FBI and University of Virginia. Unlike Heilbrun, he claimed he was not paid for his testimony and had treated several women who have killed their children.

Saathoff told the court that it was unusual that Clancy hadn't reported hearing voices before the killings and that the voices ceased afterwards. He also said he found several inconsistencies in Clancy's account of what happened.

It is well documented that Clancy needed treatment for a mental health condition, and admitted herself to McLean, a psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts, a few weeks before the murders. Testimony from expert witnesses who were called by the defense had very different conclusions about her mental state.

Dr Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist and expert in filicide, testified on Friday that Clancy was "clearly psychotic" on the day she killed her children and was not in control of her actions.

"It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings," he said.

That echoed another defense witness, Paul Zeizel, the psychologist who concluded Clancy "had no appreciation for the wrongfulness of her act".

Before the court adjourned for the day on Tuesday, Judge Sullivan told the jury that the presentation of evidence would conclude on Wednesday and that closing arguments would likely follow on Thursday. Deliberations are expected to begin on Friday. He encouraged jurors not to form their own conclusions until the very end.

"You've heard a lot of evidence, but you haven't heard all of it, right? And like I said before, you haven't heard the closing arguments of the attorneys," Sullivan said. "You haven't heard the law that you're going to have to apply to this. So you still have to keep an open mind."

In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org . In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

articles.title: Florida tourism sees decline as Canadians skip visits amid Trump trade war
articles.summary: The Canadian tourism slump has the hospitality industry worried across multiple states
articles.body:
Tourism from Canada to the U.S. has been impacted across the country amid the Trump administration's ongoing trade war with its traditional ally.

In Florida, tourism from Canada was down more than four percent in the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period in 2025.

In the first six months of this year, Canadian tourism to the Sunshine State was down nearly 14 percent, according to Visit Florida .

The drop comes as the Trump administration has spent months antagonizing Canada, typically a staunch U.S. ally and major trading partner.

The White House has launched 50 percent tariffs on Canadian products, and Canada has responded with retaliatory measures, further souring a relationship already under strain from the president's repeated suggestions the country could become the 51st state .

Researchers in Canada have identified a similar decline.

Canadian visits to U.S. metro areas fell by about 42 percent since Trump took office, experts at the University of Toronto found by analyzing cell phone data. Six of the 10 cities that have seen the largest decline in visitors from Canada were in Florida, according to the researchers, though Myrtle Beach, South Carolina topped the list.

Overall, border crossings into the U.S. from Canada were down by more than a quarter in 2025, compared with 2024, according to the Canadian government .

"Excluding the COVID-19 pandemic period, the resulting 11-month streak of year-over-year declines was the deepest and most sustained on record for border crossings from the United States," Statistics Canada wrote in July, comparing the drop in travel to the months after the 9/11 terror attack in New York City.

The impact has been felt in major tourist destinations across the country.

In Las Vegas, visits from Canada were down about 18 percent in 2025.

This August, city tourism officials went on a sales mission in Western Canada to bolster demand.

"We're here to make sure you know that we care about Canada," Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority CEO Steve Hill said at a kickoff event. "We know that Canada loves Las Vegas. We love Canada right back!"

In New York, meanwhile, Canadian tourism was down 26 percent in 2025 compared to the previous year, while spending from these tourists was down 14 percent from pre-pandemic levels.

"Our tourism economy cannot afford another year of trade wars with Canada that drive away our most important international visitors," Vijay Dandapani, president and CEO of the Hotel Association of New York City, told The City Reporter. "The federal government must reach a deal with Canada and give travelers a reason to come back. If we fail to act, New York risks losing even more visitors from our number one tourism partner."

"The federal government must reach a deal with Canada and give travelers a reason to come back. If we fail to act, New York risks losing even more visitors from our number one tourism partner."

articles.title: Congressâs pellet gun fire draws BJP 1984 counter
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Demand from opposition MPs, including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, that a parliamentary committee take up the issue of use of âexcessiveâ force a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Demand from opposition MPs, including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, that a parliamentary committee take up the issue of use of âexcessiveâ force against protesting students led to a fiery exchange at its meeting on Tuesday as a BJP member brought up the âglorificationâ of anti-Sikh riots convict Sajjan Kumar to counter the Congressâs move to raise a matter that was not part of the agenda of âcrimes against childrenâ.Sources said Congress MP Ajay Maken had written to parliamentary committee on home affairs chairperson and BJP MP Radha Mohan Das Agrawal on Aug 5 saying the discussion should include the allegations against the Delhi Police that its personnel used pellet guns and nail-fitted batons against protesting students during their march to Parliament on July 20. As the committee met, Maken raised the issue and was supported by a number of other opposition MPs, including Priyanka and Senta UBTâs Sanjay Raut. They said the Delhi Police chief should be asked to appear before the committee, insisting that the issue fell within the ambit of crimes against children.Agrawal said the matter is sub judice. With opposition MPs pressing their demand, BJP MP Tarun Chugh said that if members are allowed to raise issues not on the agenda, then he would like the committee to take up the alleged glorification of a Sikh-riots convict, a reference to former Congress MP Sajjan Kumar who died last week while serving his sentence.Chughâs remarks drew a sharp reaction from Congress MP Jai Prakash, who said the issue was not relevant at all. BJP has accused Congress MP Deepender Hooda of being laudatory in his tribute to Kumar. Hooda has rejected the charge. Agrawal managed to restore order while ruling out a discussion on issues not on the agenda, even as he added that the committee would take up at a later date the issue of SOPs for the use of force against protesters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations
articles.summary: Owner ByteDance ordered to erase illegally obtained child data in Brazil as crackdown on tech giants intensifies.
articles.body:
Brazil's data protection authority has fined TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, nearly $30m for the alleged mishandling of children and teenagers' personal data, in the nation's latest move against social media companies.

The regulatory body said in its ruling that TikTok had breached data privacy laws across both logged-in accounts and guest browsing sessions by collecting and processing young users' personal information without a valid legal basis or adequate safeguards.

The regulator estimated that TikTok may have processed the data of at least 8 million children, highlighting what they said were systemic deficiencies within the platform's age-verification mechanism.

The company can still appeal the decision in the next 10 days, according to the regulator.

The ruling also includes an order for TikTok to erase all data amassed illegally.

Brazil's regulatory authority also mandated the company to formulate an improved comprehensive youth-protection framework, stressing that TikTok's "logged-out feed", which allows users to browse content without creating an account, enables widespread use ‌of the ⁠platform by minors while bypassing age-verification checks.

According to the regulator, the feature is available in Brazil but not in the United States or Europe, where access is solely restricted to registered users.

Earlier this month, the regulator ordered the social media platform Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature across the country, accusing the platform of failing to protect children and teenagers. The move came after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide following a livestream in which authorities say she was encouraged to harm herself.

The voice and text chat app, hugely popular with gamers, launched in 2015.

Brazil's government, under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the Supreme Court have tried to regulate internet use by minors, with mixed results so far, at a moment when countries such as Australia, Canada and Indonesia are undertaking similar efforts.

articles.title: ICE arrests mother and daughter at Florida hospital after car crash
articles.summary: Agents arrest women who ‘almost died’ after they were hit by vehicle and their car flipped over four times, family say
articles.body:
An Ecuadorian mother and daughter were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) agents at a hospital after a car crash in central Florida.

On 20 August, Grace Stephanie Calero Cabanilla, 39, and her daughter, Giulianna Mía Carriel Calero, 19, were involved in a car crash in Poinciana, Florida, according to arrest reports reviewed by multiple news outlets.

According to Jonathan Bravo, Calero Cabanilla's cousin, who spoke to Newsweek , she was driving to work with her daughter when another vehicle struck the passenger side of their car, in which the pair "almost died" after the car flipped over four times.

Pictures of the crash posted by Bravo on a fundraiser showed a black SUV with damage to both the front and rear.

After Calero Cabanilla and her daughter were transported by ambulance to HCA Florida Poinciana hospital, they were placed in separate rooms, Bravo told Newsweek. He said a Polk county sheriff's deputy then began asking Calero Cabanilla about her immigration status.

Video posted online by Gia Calero, Calero Cabanilla's sister, and published by CNN showed the two women embracing in tears on a hospital bed as law enforcement officers attempted to separate them. The video also showed officers with Calero Cabanilla's hands behind her back as she cried out while they escorted her from the hospital room. A person who appeared to be filming the video could be heard asking: "Where's the paper? Where's the arrest warrant?"

In a statement to Newsweek, a Polk county sheriff's office spokesperson said: "As part of a crash investigation on Thursday, deputies went to the local hospital to speak with the occupants of one of the vehicles … As the deputies were obtaining information from those involved, it was discovered that the driver is in the United States illegally from Ecuador after overstaying an expired visa by several years."

The sheriff's office added that it determined Calero had also overstayed her visa, saying: "ICE issued detainers for both women, and after the women were discharged from the hospital, they were taken into custody and transported to the Polk County Jail." An arrest warrant reviewed by Newsweek showed that neither woman had a criminal history.

The Guardian has reached out to the Polk county sheriff's office and ICE for additional comment.

Meanwhile, in the fundraiser set up for the pair, Bravo said that Calero Cabanilla has a pending asylum case and a work permit, while her daughter has a visa that is valid until 2030. The Guardian has contacted Bravo for additional comment.

The arrests of the mother and daughter come amid a series of recent ICE arrests that have sparked widespread criticism across the country. Those arrested include the father of a USS Lincoln sailor, who was taken into ICE detention while his son was deployed in the Middle East, though since released , as well as several higher education instructors and researchers in recent weeks.

The arrests have drawn particular criticism in light of Donald Trump administration's repeated pledge to focus on targeting the "worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens" for arrest and deportation.

A Guardian analysis published in February found that 77% of people placed into deportation proceedings for the first time after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 had no criminal convictions.
